title: What a game can tell us about a troubling economic trend
gist: Even Major League Baseball players, one of the most unionized and 'AI-proof' workforces in the world, have seen their share of league revenue decline since the early 2000s, illustrating a broader global trend of labour's falling share of economic output that the Bank for International Settlements warns AI could push as low as 20% in coming decades.

insights.claim: The Bank for International Settlements has projected that labour's global share of income could fall as low as 20% in the coming decades, with artificial intelligence accelerating the decline.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A BIS forecast of a structurally shrinking labour share versus capital/owner share implies durable margin and capital-income tailwinds for owners of productive assets relative to wage earners, reinforcing overweight-capital, underweight-labour positioning theses.
insights.quote: it could fall as low as 20% in the next few decades, with artificial intelligence speeding the decline.

insights.claim: Labour's share of global economic output has been slipping since the start of the 21st century, and while economists debate the exact causes, there is broad consensus it matters because it signals rising inequality.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Widespread expert agreement that a falling labour share is a real, consequential inequality indicator (not just a statistical artifact) supports policy and market narratives around redistribution, wage-growth stagnation, and populist political risk.
insights.quote: Economists debate exactly why it’s happening and to what extent, but most agree that it matters.

insights.claim: Major League Baseball players are a highly unionized, relatively automation-resistant ('AI-proof') labour force, yet they still could not buck the global decline in labour's share of income, suggesting the trend is structural rather than confined to jobs vulnerable to automation.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: If even strongly unionized, automation-resistant labour can't hold its income share, investors should not assume AI-safe or heavily unionized sectors will be immune to the broader wage-share compression theme when modeling labour cost and margin trends.
insights.locator: Players in baseball's premier professional league

themes.theme: MLB labor economics and the salary-cap standoff

insights.claim: In 1883, the average American professional baseball player earned about $2,000 a year (roughly $66,000 in today's dollars), and needed off-season jobs like factory work to make ends meet, until the players' union secured its first collective bargaining agreement in 1968, which raised minimum pay and paved the way for free agency.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Shows how collective bargaining historically converted a low-pay, side-hustle-dependent labour pool into a high-earning one via structural changes (free agency) rather than incremental wage demands — a template for how labour can capture more of surplus value when it gains bargaining leverage.
insights.locator: Karl Marx might have been a baseball fan

insights.claim: The average MLB salary has risen to $5.3 million this year, but an academic study found players' share of overall league income began declining in the early 2000s and the slump appears to be continuing despite rising nominal pay.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Illustrates that rising absolute compensation can mask a falling share of the value being created — a distinction investors should apply when assessing whether wage growth in any sector is actually keeping pace with revenue/profit growth.
insights.locator: The average salary for Major League Baseball players this year

insights.claim: MLB team owners are proposing a salary cap ahead of a December labor-deal deadline, risking a work stoppage; economics professor Michael Haupert argues the cap would not just constrain top salaries but squeeze compensation at every level of the pay scale.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A December deadline with real work-stoppage risk is a concrete, dated catalyst for MLB-adjacent businesses (media rights, sponsorships, the publicly traded Atlanta Braves) — investors should track negotiation progress into year-end.
insights.quote: not just squeeze the highest salaries, it will squeeze all the way down
insights.locator: That's still probably fallen behind the pace of league proceeds

insights.claim: Despite a wide pay gap between the league minimum ($780,000) and the top salary this year ($61.9 million), rank-and-file players and superstars are reported to be equally opposed to a salary cap.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Unified opposition across the pay spectrum strengthens the union's negotiating leverage against owners, making a prolonged dispute or work stoppage more likely than if lower-paid members were more willing to compromise.
insights.locator: Members at the bottom of the pay scale

insights.claim: Player compensation is increasingly shaped by granular, quantified performance metrics — such as launch angle and pitch spin rate, plus a proprietary statistic designed to detect the earliest signs of skill decline — that directly affect market value, paralleling how AI-powered workplace monitoring ('bossware') is increasingly tracking white-collar employees.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Signals that granular performance-tracking technology used in sports analytics is a preview of AI-driven surveillance/evaluation tools spreading into mainstream white-collar workplaces, with implications for both HR-tech vendors and worker bargaining power.
insights.locator: Office workers fret about having more of their day tracked by AI-powered

insights.claim: The Atlanta Braves are the only MLB team required to disclose extensive financial information because they are publicly traded, and their stock has recently seen elevated short interest amid investor skepticism about the outcome of the new labour deal.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The Braves' public listing makes it a rare direct market proxy for MLB labor-negotiation risk; rising short interest is a live, trackable signal of investor sentiment on the salary-cap dispute and potential work stoppage.
insights.quote: the public has been shorting those shares lately, or betting against them, amid scepticism about a new labour deal
insights.locator: Only one club, the Atlanta Braves

insights.claim: Ancillary team revenue such as real estate development near ballparks (e.g., the Atlanta Braves' residential building and hotel named after Hank Aaron) raises an unresolved question of whether players are entitled to a share of that income, which Haupert calls 'a legitimate question.'
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Ancillary/real-estate revenue streams sit outside traditional baseball-related-revenue definitions used in labor deals, making them a plausible future flashpoint in collective bargaining as owners diversify income beyond ticket and media sales.
insights.locator: Real estate near a ballpark can earn income for a team

insights.claim: The Los Angeles Angels were sold for a record $4 billion, up from $183 million when they were sold in 2003 — roughly a 22x increase in franchise value over 23 years, far outpacing growth in player pay share.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Franchise valuations compounding at a much faster rate than players' share of league revenue is direct quantitative evidence that capital (team ownership) is capturing a growing share of the value created relative to labour.
insights.locator: The Los Angeles Angels were sold last week

insights.claim: The Angels' payroll of $179 million is far below the largest MLB payrolls, which exceed $300 million, yet it is not clear that bigger payrolls provide a decisive competitive advantage, undercutting owners' argument that a salary cap is needed for competitive balance.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Weakens the owners' stated rationale for a salary cap, suggesting the real driver of the cap push is capturing a larger share of league revenue rather than competitive parity — useful framing for assessing negotiation motives and likely outcomes.
insights.quote: far below the largest at well over $300 million
insights.locator: The Angels have a middling payroll

insights.claim: Some of the highest-performing baseball talent in history was systematically underpaid because team owners colluded to exclude black players from the major leagues via the segregated 'Negro Leagues' until 1947.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A historical case study showing that engineered labor-market segmentation, not just lack of skill or bargaining power, can suppress even top-tier compensation — a cautionary precedent when evaluating claims that wage gaps reflect merit alone.
insights.quote: Some of the highest-performing employees in history were underpaid because owners could collude to marginalize black baseball talent until 1947.
insights.locator: Another connection between ballplayers and the broader workforce

insights.claim: Before free agency, MLB owners colluded to restrict players to a single employer, arguing that allowing players to freely change teams would ruin the game — a restriction later broken by the 1968 collective bargaining agreement.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that employer-side collusion to limit worker mobility was a deliberate wage-suppression mechanism, historically justified with competitive/quality arguments similar to those now used to justify the proposed salary cap.
insights.locator: The lack of free agency in the old days

insights.claim: After a 1981 work stoppage, MLB ran a 'blow the whistle on the players' fan campaign at the first game back, but a broadcaster noted fans couldn't similarly whistle at the owners because they weren't present, exposing an asymmetry in how labor disputes get publicly framed against workers rather than owners.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A recurring PR pattern — labor disputes get framed as player/worker greed while owners remain comparatively shielded from public blame — is a useful lens for interpreting media narratives around the looming December MLB negotiation and work-stoppage risk.
insights.quote: You can’t very well whistle on the owners, they’re not here.
insights.locator: After a work stoppage erased part of the 1981 season

insights.claim: According to Haupert, most workers don't think about their compensation in terms of a target percentage of total revenue, instead prioritizing the freedom to leave one job for a better one — a framing gap that may help explain why labour's declining income share persists without organized resistance.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: If workers don't benchmark pay against revenue share, erosion in labour's share can continue largely unchallenged; making that metric more visible (as this article attempts) could itself become a catalyst for renewed wage-share demands or policy attention.
insights.quote: I don’t think the average worker really goes into things thinking, 'I should have X-percent of the total revenue'
insights.locator: That's a potential misread of human nature by Marx
